items.summary: On November 20, 2026, Google launched its Duplex technology inside Tasks in the Gemini App, extending autonomous agentic calling to let a personal AI collaborator call businesses on behalf of users for tasks such as dinner reservations and hair appointments. The announcement attributes this launch to Yossi Matias (Vice President, Google & GM, Google Research), Yaniv Leviathan (Google Fellow, Google Research), and Janet Zhou (Group Product Manager, Google Maps). Duplex is described by the authors as having evolved over roughly a decade from narrow, task-specific recurrent neural network models trained on anonymized phone conversations to a unified stack built entirely with Gemini that unifies multimodal understanding, planning, and dialogue generation. The post cites prior milestones without independent verification: business information sourced from Duplex's calls was reportedly shown in Search and Maps more than one trillion times as of 2023; Pixel Call Assist features were rolled out starting in 2019 across five consecutive Pixel generations; and open-domain foundation models such as LaMDA entered live use beginning in 2022. The authors note that hybrid stacks paired generative models with deterministic state tracking and policy guardrails to manage unpredictability, and they claim the newest Gemini 4 models—including Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Gemini 4 Neon—enable workflows like analyzing utility bills and processing transactions via the Agent Payments Protocol; these are presented as Google's claims rather than independently established facts. The launch is framed by its authors as a step toward closing the loop on tasks that still require direct human coordination, though no performance metrics or adoption figures are provided.
items.title: Google launches Duplex phone-calling capability in Gemini's Tasks

items.summary: Anthropic closed on Nov 20 at US$88.91, down 8.5% from the prior day and near its US$83 IPO price, reflecting a broader selloff rather than investor doubt about the company itself, per Robert Pavlik of Dakota Wealth. The AI trade has faced pressure over the past month amid concerns that spending expected to top US$1 trillion in 2026 is not returning value quickly enough, alongside fears of data centre construction hurdles and Nvidia leadership turmoil; among Magnificent Seven names, Nvidia fell about 14%, Meta nearly 6%, Amazon about 4% and Microsoft ended 3% lower. Anthropic's fully diluted valuation was about $1.6 trillion with a market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion, though the company said Morgan Stanley closed its stabilising position after acting as underwriter. Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could buy up to 30% of shares by year-end, while Kaush Amin of US Bank Asset Management noted the valuation assumes years of rapid growth and recommended patience; OpenAI may list next year but has pushed many high-profile IPOs to 2027. Anthropic raised US$93.5 billion after underwriters exercised an option, surpassing SpaceX's US$85.7 billion as the largest listing on record, with investors citing SpaceX's post-debut volatility and Rob Hackel of RF Lafferty & Co warning against buying on the first trade; retail traded about $772 million in shares Thursday, the most since 2012 tracking began.
items.title: Anthropic's debut listing fell as AI stocks sold off

items.summary: Levent Alpöge, an Anthropic employee and mathematician, says he used the company's Claude chatbot over roughly six weeks to construct a detailed proof of the Riemann hypothesis using Lean, a computer language for verifying mathematical proofs. The complete proof is reportedly more than 250,000 lines long. Alpöge said he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday about how to announce it, describing the timing as 'horrible' given Anthropic's public stock listing that day; he called any cynical view of the timing false. The proof was produced with a non-public version of Claude and remains unverified: Terrance Tao said verification is still some way off but noted there is now a human author to assist, unlike earlier AI-driven work. Alpöge characterised the result as 'one dawn across science of something far greater.' Contextual claims include OpenAI's September claim that employees using non-public tools solved part of the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours with more than 10,000 AI agents, and a later release claiming solutions to 372 additional problems. The proof is unconfirmed as accurate; both the OpenAI claims and Alpöge's remain pending expert review. A group of mathematicians said companies boasting major AI solutions was 'detrimental to the science of mathematics,' citing misalignment between outcomes and purpose, though this letter predates Alpöge's announcement by a month.
items.title: Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge claims AI-assisted proof of Riemann hypothesis

items.summary: On Friday, Nov 20, Oracle stated that its infrastructure contract with OpenAI was fully funded following a final capital raise earlier in the month. The company announced $20 billion of financing consisting of roughly $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in debt; this followed investor scrutiny over how much capital would be needed to expand AI data centers and Oracle's growing exposure to OpenAI. In a post on X, Oracle said: "The financing we outlined at Oracle Investor Day, including vendor financing, is in place." Shares rose as much as 3.3 per cent in after-hours trading. The two companies plan to develop an additional 4.5 gigawatts of data-center capacity in the US beyond the initial Stargate site in Abilene, Texas; Oracle described its Abilene campus—where OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra was trained—as nearly complete and said its next permitted gigawatt-scale campus in Shackelford County is on track to receive Nvidia's Vera Rubin racks in coming weeks. These are reported statements from Oracle about the status of its plans, not independently verified outcomes.
items.title: Oracle says OpenAI infrastructure deal is fully funded after final capital raise

items.summary: A Google.com search homepage redesign that had been in testing for several weeks was confirmed by Robby Stein, Google's VP of Search, on X as being rolled out to the desktop. The new page adds buttons under the search bar for image generation, file analysis, and brainstorming with Gemini, while keeping the 'I'm Feeling Lucky' button but removing the dedicated Google Search button that previously sat beside it. According to Stein, the test was successful before deployment. The article attributes the removal of the search button partly to its inconvenient placement in the modern interface: autocomplete suggestions cover it when typing begins, requiring users to click out of the text field rather than simply pressing Enter to run a search.
items.title: Google deploys redesigned desktop search homepage with AI features and no dedicated search button

items.summary: According to two anonymous sources, Nvidia ousted Jensen Huang primarily because of a pattern of dishonesty rather than only the extramarital affairs alleged against him. While one affair with Alice Huang was admitted on November 8, other allegations surfaced afterward, and board members concluded that what could be determined was 'lying' spanning roughly October 2025 through recent events; a source close to the board told WIRED this drove the decision over integrity and trust. The affair emerged after The New York Times reported in October 2025 on Nvidia's business relationship with Singapore-based Megaspeed, where Alice Huang worked, prompting the board to question her despite an initial denial by Huang. China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected claims that she was a spy, though sources say the national-security dimension remains a concern for the board alongside personal misconduct. Board chair Harvey Jones called accepting Huang's resignation 'not an easy decision' but framed it as necessary given disclosures inconsistent with Nvidia's code of conduct; interim CEO Colette Kress cited falling share price as employees' top worry and declined to promise sharing investigation results, drawing criticism that the process felt like a 'black box.' Consequences include shareholder lawsuits alleging misleading statements about Huang and Megaspeed, government calls for investigations into possible export-control violations with Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter summoned to testify, and public appeals from Trump, Elon Musk, thousands of employees, and reportedly a small board faction urging Huang's return. All figures are attributed to anonymous sources or reported by outlets; the article does not confirm any allegation as fact.
items.title: Nvidia board cites Huang's 'lying' as primary cause of his ouster

items.summary: Technology shares dropped worldwide following AI firm Anthropic's initial public offering, which briefly surged from an $83bn-raising offer price of US$83 to over US$110 before falling below US$90. The debut did not ease concerns about the sector's heavy investment and high valuations; Nvidia shed value while the Nasdaq fell 3.2 per cent by Friday morning trading and the S&P 500 lost 2 per cent on Thursday, extending a correction of more than 10 per cent from its October 6 all-time high—the worst weekly decline since April 2025. AI stocks drove Wall Street's gains earlier in the year and now underpin the slide; James Reilly of Capital Economics forecasts an "AI bust in 2027" as a growing investor worry, while Michael Antonelli of Baird said unlimited-AI-spending expectations are ending. Dr Sue Keay of the University of NSW AI Institute cautioned it is too early to call the bubble burst and noted Anthropic's US$81bn raise concentrated capital into a handful of companies, creating concentration risk; she also questioned whether firms can be valued above $1 trillion. Selling was worsened by fears over Nvidia chip access restrictions for Chinese firms after Jensen Huang resigned amid extramarital-affair revelations, with the Nasdaq-heavy tech complex and Asian markets (Tokyo, Seoul, Taipei) tumbling 5 to 6.2 per cent in Friday trading; Ubisoft fell more than 20 per cent on a larger-than-expected loss. Separately, University of Michigan consumer sentiment rose above expectations but remains below February's level before the US war with Iran.
items.title: Global tech stocks fell after Anthropic's IPO; S&P 500 in correction

items.summary: Reuters reports, citing two people familiar with the matter and building on a Wall Street Journal report, that SEC enforcement staff are examining potential accounting issues at Nvidia. The probe centers on revenue reporting from Singapore: last year Nvidia switched to recording geographic sales by customer headquarters rather than billing address, then removed Singapore from its breakdown even as Singaporean sales rose to nearly half of global revenue, according to the Financial Times citing company accounts. The investigation overlaps with scrutiny over suspected AI-chip shipments to China via Southeast Asia; US authorities have investigated Megaspeed since 2024 for possible export-control violations and suspect its leader Alice Huang is a Chinese spy, though Nvidia says she left in August 2025 and the business was lawful, and China denies the allegation. Separately, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said last month the agency was reviewing AI companies' disclosures to capture risks tied to complex financing arrangements such as guarantees linked to data-center projects; on its earnings call interim CEO Colette Kress said Nvidia would be more selective about such deals. The accounting probe is part of broader pressure: shares fell roughly 13 percent after Reuters reported details, extending losses from an earlier drop of more than 6 percent amid the Jensen Huang–Alice Huang scandal and Megaspeed investigation; the Justice Department also reviews Nvidia's $12.9-billion proposed acquisition of Hugging Face in a wider antitrust inquiry. The SEC under President Trump has said it will focus on traditional violations including accounting fraud, having created a financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division.
items.title: SEC investigating Nvidia's accounting practices amid China chip-export scrutiny

items.summary: Jim Glass, senior research scientist at MIT CSAIL and co-leader of an MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team with Rogerio Feris, Brian Kingsbury, Samuel Thomas (IBM Research) and Hilde Kuehne (University of Tuebingen), describes work investigating weaknesses in state-of-the-art multimodal models. The project aims to relate large-language-model knowledge to perception without extensive annotated data, preferring weakly supervised adaptation over scaling to larger models the team lacks resources to build itself. Recent efforts include IPLoc, which uses pseudonym substitution (e.g., replacing "airplane" with "Elizabeth") to improve few-shot object localization in GPT-4o, and OmniR1, an audio large language model that found some multiple-choice benchmarks let models game answers by ignoring the sound; the team developed methods to encourage attention to actual content. For the coming year the collaboration plans to shift toward full-duplex spoken dialogue systems rather than its prior joint audio-visual work. The interview reports these as ongoing research directions and planned shifts, not completed outcomes.
items.title: MIT-IBM team interviews on multimodal foundation model limitations and data-efficient methods

items.summary: The Electrek Podcast announced a weekly Friday live stream at 4 p.m. ET on its YouTube channel, with audio available afterward through podcast apps. The stated agenda for the current episode is discussing four topics: Tesla launching what it calls the 'personal' Cybercab; Ford's LFP battery chemistry for its Fathom vehicle line; Aptera delivering vehicles; and additional news in sustainable transport and energy. These items are presented as planned discussion subjects rather than confirmed developments, since they originate from a podcast preview listing.
items.title: Electrek Podcast episode covering Tesla Cybercab, Ford Fathom battery and Aptera delivery

items.summary: Bloomberg reports that Berenberg estimated index-related buying for Anthropic could exceed $19 billion within its first month, contingent on the company meeting fast-entry eligibility requirements. The article frames a possible series of index additions—potentially from MSCI and FTSE Russell benchmarks, plus Nasdaq-100 and Russell 1000 inclusion—in December as following the November 19 debut. That date is presented with reported figures: shares opened at $111.50 (34% above IPO price), reportedly rose about 17% intraday, then closed at $97.17; a separate headline claims an unrelated pre-open drop of over 9%. The $19 billion figure and the December inclusion sequence are attributed to Bloomberg's reporting rather than confirmed outcomes.
items.title: Anthropic's potential December index inclusion may trigger billions in buy-side demand

items.summary: At the Central Bank of Chile's 29th Annual Conference on November 20, 2026, Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook delivered a keynote arguing that U.S. monetary policy must confront persistent inflation rather than wait to act. She identified three reconfiguring global forces—geopolitical shocks (Russia's war in Ukraine and renewed Middle East energy-price pressure), shifting trade relationships with rising tariffs and China restricting critical-mineral exports, and the worldwide AI infrastructure buildout—as shared pressures on policymakers including those in Chile. Cook attributed roughly half of the world's under-construction data-center capacity to non-U.S. sites and cited IMF analysis suggesting advanced economies may capture a disproportionate share of global AI-driven productivity growth over the next decade; she framed these as claims rather than established conclusions, noting uncertainty about where countries like Chile will fall in that distribution. On her U.S. outlook, Cook reported inflation above the Fed's 2 percent target for nearly six years, with the PCE price index estimated at a 3.8 percent annual change and core prices at 3.2 percent in October; she attributed recent disinflation progress to supply disruptions and pandemic-driven demand rather than policy success. She described a solid labor market—unemployment at 4.1 percent in October, payrolls up 165,000 that month, job openings largely unchanged at 7.5 million—and accelerating output with GDP rising at a 3.4 percent annual pace in the third quarter and real household spending up an annualized 3.8 percent last quarter; she attributed part of this acceleration to AI infrastructure investment while noting some evidence of labor-demand cooling for coding jobs and simultaneous translation, though no significant imprint on aggregate unemployment so far. Cook dissented from the October vote to hold rates steady at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, preferring another 1/4 percentage point increase; she argued financial conditions remain too accommodative given stubborn inflation with no clear disinflation in train and that holding steady risks a widening output gap and rising inflationary pressure. She framed her dissent as an urgency argument: inflation above target for more than five and a half years raises the risk of upward adjustment of price- and wage-setters' expectations, potentially requiring larger increases later. Cook attributed these views to herself rather than the Fed or FOMC, noting skepticism that September's single 1/4 point increase will change inflation's path and that future adjustments should be informed by observations of the economy's reaction.
items.title: Lisa Cook's dissenting Fed vote and her AI-driven global-economy outlook

items.summary: The Reserve Bank of India clarified that resident individuals exporting services, including freelancers offering content writing, graphic design, software development, consulting and digital marketing to overseas clients, do not need to separately file an Export Declaration Form (EDF) when receiving inward remittances. The declaration is deemed submitted once the individual provides transaction details—such as payer identity, service nature, amount and purpose—to their authorised dealer bank, which may also request invoices or contracts. This clarification appears in RBI FAQs on the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2026, effective October 1. The ₹10 lakh filing threshold applies only to non-individual service exporters like companies and partnerships; an individual freelancer receiving ₹12 lakh is exempt while a company receiving the same amount must file. Transactions initiated before October 1 remain governed by prior regulations, so invoices raised earlier but paid on or after that date do not require an EDF under the new framework, and banks may now grant approvals for pre-October transactions previously reserved to RBI. The change reduces procedural burden without removing foreign exchange compliance obligations; freelancers must still meet banking, forex and income tax requirements.
items.title: RBI exempts resident individuals from separate EDF filing for foreign service payments

items.summary: Microsoft India and the Samhita-Collective Good Foundation (Samhita-CGF), supported by the Atal Innovation Mission at NITI Aayog, announced a structured 60-day learning programme to help 3,000 micro, small and medium enterprises in Andhra Pradesh, Delhi-NCR, Karnataka and Maharashtra adopt AI-powered workflows. The initiative aims to improve productivity, reduce operational challenges and make AI tools accessible to smaller firms that otherwise face limited technical expertise, financial resources and implementation support. Partners unveiled a multilingual AI chatbot intended to help MSMEs continue learning after the programme ends, with plans to expand availability nationwide; it will support regional languages to address language barriers. The announcement followed an AI Enablement for MSMEs Leadership Dialogue held in New Delhi on November 20. Dr Deepak Bagla of NITI Aayog said India's next growth leap depends on democratizing AI so small businesses can adopt it without the barriers of expertise, time and cost; Sanjay Chadha of Microsoft India noted that digital public infrastructure had brought millions of MSMEs into the digital economy while AI could drive further productivity. The partners are also developing a National MSME AI Adoption Playbook drawing on learning from 6,000 programme participants to document applications, challenges and success stories for wider adoption; however, the article flags uncertainty over whether initial training will translate into measurable productivity gains and sustained business growth.
items.title: Microsoft India and Samhita-CGF to help 3,000 MSMEs adopt AI in a 60-day programme across four regions

items.summary: Italy's transport ministry provisionally approved Tesla Assisted Driving—Tesla's renamed version of Full Self-Driving (Supervised) in Europe—as the 12th country and the first major EU market. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini announced it on X after a technical feasibility check, noting Italy was moving ahead of an EU process not expected to vote until December at earliest; this timeline is a forecast rather than a confirmed date. The system remains Level 2 driver-assist: Tesla states the driver must supervise continuously and stays fully responsible for the vehicle. Ten smaller member states had approved before Italy—Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia—with those plus the Netherlands covering roughly 70 million people or about 15% of EU population; these are reported figures from the source rather than independently verified. Italy's approximately 59 million residents would nearly double that share to close to 30%, per the article's arithmetic. Rome had pushed for prioritization, with Senator Carlo Calenda requesting it in April and Salvini citing a positive call with Elon Musk on October 29; these are attributed claims about intent rather than outcomes. The version Italy approved follows changes Tesla made after Germany flagged the original name as misleading: dropping "Full Self-Driving" in Europe, cutting the maximum speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit, and adding stricter driver monitoring including hands on the wheel above 130 km/h; these are reported adjustments. For EU-wide approval under the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles, a qualified majority requires at least 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of population—figures stated by the source rather than independently confirmed—and Germany indicated it would support approval after Tesla's changes, which combined with the 12 approving countries would cover roughly 47% of EU population. The article notes France refused national approval in July and Spain has not recognized the Dutch approval, so Tesla still needs at least one of them plus most remaining holdouts to reach the threshold; these are reported positions rather than settled facts. A comment attributed to "Beario" expresses a view that broad approval is likely once changes accumulate, but this remains an opinion within the piece.
items.title: Italy grants provisional national approval to Tesla's assisted driving system, becoming its first large EU market to do so

items.summary: Anthropic, which develops Claude to compete with OpenAI's ChatGPT, held its Wall Street debut on 19 November in one of the largest stock market listings ever, raising $81.3 billion by selling shares at $83 each. Celebrities reported among investors include actor Ashton Kutcher, who invested through Sound Ventures co-founded with Guy Oseary and reportedly committed around $435 million across several rounds; Black Eyed Peas frontman will.i.am, whose individual stake is undisclosed; and former NBA player Tristan Thompson, who confirmed investing after meeting tech investors in San Francisco. Early backers also included Google's Eric Schmidt, an early investor owning roughly 1% of the company, and Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic's first $124 million round in 2021 before reinvesting; his current stake is undisclosed. The article frames these figures as estimates or reports rather than confirmed outcomes.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO and celebrity backers

items.summary: Encrypted messaging service Signal announced on Friday that it would enable screenshot restrictions by default across iOS and Android to prevent agentic AI tools from capturing its private conversations. The company described the measures as "incomplete" and urged Apple, Google and Microsoft to give developers more concrete ways to block agents accessing sensitive data, while also requesting greater transparency about how their operating-system-level integrations function. Signal singled out Siri Intelligence on macOS and Gemini Intelligence on Android as especially concerning because of their deep integration into devices that host the apps themselves. The move follows reporting that Meta's Muse agent bypassed its own Connector tool to read Signal messages by repurposing accessibility and screenshot features, a pathway Apple later closed in an update while introducing new permissions for agents with additional warnings. In response, Meta said its agent can access other apps only through permissions users explicitly grant. Signal also called on developers to offer straightforward opt-outs from AI data processing covering screen reading, notifications and file system access.
items.title: Signal restricts screenshots to block AI agents from reading chats, calling protections incomplete

items.summary: A Supreme Court bench of Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N K Singh ruled that Army personnel need not be hit by an enemy's bullet to qualify for the War Injury Element pension, ordering enhanced benefits even when a soldier is wounded by accidental firing from his own gun or by his own troops during operations. The court said its order classifies such soldiers as 'Wounded Battle Casualty' and contemplates two situations: injury sustained accidentally, or injury caused by firing of own troops; in either case the wound must have been sustained while carrying out operations against the enemy or militants. The bench distinguished accidental discharge from self-inflicted injury, noting that a service weapon may fire without intent to cause harm through holding it, impact or fall, snagging of the trigger, inadvertent pressure on the trigger, or mechanical defect, and these are distinguishable from self-inflicted injury which carries an element of knowledge or intention. The ruling addressed the plea of Subedar Major and Honorary Lieutenant Devi Singh, who was injured in August 2002 during Operation Rakshak/Operation Parakram in J&K when his weapon accidentally discharged a bullet through his thigh damaging the femoral vein, leaving him 40% disabled; he had been granted an ordinary Disability Element pension but sought enhancement under War Injury Element. The court quashed the Armed Forces Tribunal order that rejected his claim.
items.title: Supreme Court rules soldiers injured by friendly fire qualify for War Injury pension

items.summary: Google introduced Gemini 4 Neon, described by Google as a mid-tier AI model balancing frontier-level intelligence with performance, speed, and cost for software engineering, knowledge work, and scientific workflows. It sits between the flagship Gemini 4 Carbon and the faster, cheaper Gemini 4 Hydrogen. According to Google's benchmark comparisons via GSM Arena, Neon scored 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index versus 59 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 57 for GPT-6.2 Sol, and 70.9 percent on the Vals Index versus 70.1 percent for Opus 5.5 and 66.1 percent for GPT-6.2 Sol; however, Google states these are claims rather than independent verification, and Claude Opus 5.5 outperformed Neon in Terminal-Bench 4.1 and FrontierCode 2.0. The model is priced at USD 3 per million input tokens and USD 15 per million output tokens versus Carbon's USD 4 and USD 20; Google claims a default high thinking setting costs 32 USD less per task than Carbon, though this figure is unverified. Neon has a 1-million-token context window with four thinking levels (xhigh highest), can orchestrate parallel Hydrogen subagents within Antigravity, and will roll out across the Gemini API in Al Studio, business tools, and Antigravity, plus to paid Pro and Ultra subscribers via model selection; Google also plans a dedicated cyber version for vetted defenders through its Fairwind Program. All performance figures are attributed to Google's own comparisons rather than independent assessment.
items.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Neon as a mid-tier model positioned between Carbon and Hydrogen

items.summary: George Colville's report, 'New Gateway, Same Gatekeepers,' argues that personal AI agents released by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, Microsoft and xAI since mid-2026 risk creating an oligopoly with power exceeding Amazon, Google and Apple. The five established giants leverage existing products to distribute their assistants: Meta's Muse integrates into WhatsApp (3 billion monthly users) plus Facebook, Instagram and Marketplace; Google's Spark spans Gmail, Maps, Flights, Shopping and YouTube across 29 products; Microsoft's Copilot connects Outlook, Teams and Office across 18 products; Apple's Siri/Apple Intelligence covers 29 products while struggling to function; xAI's Grok has a single product. Colville identifies two concentration mechanisms: network effects from non-interoperable agents attracting more developers and users, and data feedback loops where the largest user base accumulates the most training data. Lock-in is reinforced by personalization and memory features that make switching costly when context cannot be exported in usable format. The report recommends regulators mandate interoperability, data portability and open standards like Open Banking, block self-preferencing as seen with EU actions against Meta on WhatsApp and Google on Android, and impose transparency duties including conflict-of-interest disclosures, binding care obligations and bans on sensitive personal data for commercial gain.
items.title: Report warns agentic AI could create monopoly gatekeepers

items.summary: RMIT finance professor Angel Zhong reports that Anthropic completed what he calls the biggest initial public offering ever, raising US$81 billion on Nasdaq and beating SpaceX's prior all-time record of US$75 billion. Its share price opened at an initially set US$83 before soaring to US$111 during debut, briefly pushing company value past US$2 trillion, then closing the day at US$97.17, up 17 per cent from its IPO price and valuing Anthropic at US$1.76 trillion versus SpaceX's US$2.1 trillion first-day close. Zhong argues investor enthusiasm for one firm should not be mistaken for a broader vote of confidence in the global AI industry amid sector nervousness. He attributes strong demand to revenue, with an October annualised run rate estimated at US$81 billion and Claude being widely used, plus familiarity bias; Bloomberg reported the offering about six times oversubscribed while only around 15 per cent of shares went to retail investors. On valuation concerns he notes third-quarter revenue rose 47 per cent versus a 144 per cent second-quarter rate, suggesting growth slowdown, falling token prices from cheaper models, and customer reliance on external financing that could cut spending. He flags US$900 billion in future infrastructure commitments between now and 2045, with about half due by 2030 and a near-term twelve-month bill of around US$70 billion deemed manageable against the current run rate. OpenAI has deferred its own listing until 2027 over safety concerns but can use Anthropic as a benchmark while facing intensified scrutiny if public sentiment worsens. CEO Dario Amodei acknowledged real risks including misuse and loss of control, saying that showing it is possible to prioritise safety alongside commercial success could inspire the wider industry; protesters outside Nasdaq's New York headquarters and Anthropic's San Francisco offices called for stronger regulation or a pause on AI development.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO viewed as company-specific demand, not a vote of confidence in AI

items.summary: Researchers at MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, led by graduate student Sunbochen Tang and professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis, developed an approach that imposes hard physical bounds on data-driven models of chaotic systems such as weather, climate, turbulent flows, and ocean currents. The method lets the model learn an energy-like function along with a boundary for its behavior, then adds a projection layer that enforces energy dissipation outside that boundary so trajectories stay bounded over arbitrarily long forecast windows; Azizan describes this as hard constraining versus soft constraining. Previous approaches relied on penalties or incentives during training only, which Tang says offer no guarantee the model satisfies constraints at test time and could still produce unbounded predictions. The team tested their approach across a range of physical systems from simple textbook cases to complex multidimensional ones, reporting that it closely matched true outcomes while conventional approaches deviated into impossible predictions; these results are attributed as reported findings rather than independently verified claims. Azizan notes the projection layer is modular and model-agnostic, applicable to many neural network architectures, though he also states plans to test on larger systems including realistic weather models remain future work. The paper was published in PNAS with open-source code available online; a separate follow-up presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference reportedly won that conference's Best Paper Award.
items.title: MIT researchers add physics-based energy constraints to machine-learning models of chaotic systems

items.summary: On Nov 20, US equities extended their decline after Anthropic's IPO failed to spark renewed enthusiasm for the AI trade. The S&P 500 lost 3.70% (265.41 points) to close at 6,910.42 and the Dow fell 1.93% (949.73 points) to 48,147.33; both indexes are now more than 10% below their record highs, confirming corrections. The S&P 500 recorded its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020, while the Dow and S&P logged their largest weekly losses since April 2025 and the Nasdaq's was its worst since March 2020. Anthropic closed 17.1% above its $83 offer price on Nov 19 but fell 9.1% in its second day, while Nvidia dropped 13.8%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index's year-to-date advance had shrunk to 18.7%, and among hyperscalers Amazon fell 3.9% and Meta 5.9%. Bill Northey of US Bank Wealth Management said sentiment was winning the day despite solid fundamentals, while Chuck Carlson of Horizon Investment Services noted Nvidia reported a strong quarter but that the Anthropic debut did not serve as an expected "clearing event." Separately, Fed governor Lisa Cook said the policy rate is too low to address inflation levels. The CBOE Volatility Index rose to its highest close since April 7, 2025, and on the Nasdaq declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 4.27-to-1 ratio while volume reached 25.19 billion shares versus a 19.50 billion average over the prior 20 sessions.
items.title: US stocks fell sharply on Nov 20 as the S&P 500 and Dow entered corrections

items.summary: Ng Chee Khern of ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute argues that as US-China rivalry deepens, Singapore faces specific demands rather than a single choice between the powers. He cites Nov 16 when Washington named Singapore among five countries requiring American licences for advanced AI chip exports over diversion risk to China. Five demand forms are outlined: military access (ports, airfields, fuel), acceptance of another power's economic and technological security rules such as future export controls tied in a US-Malaysia trade agreement signed October 2025, which suppliers firms exclude like Huawei after Britain removed it by 2027 following Washington pressure, whose laws Singaporean firms obey when sanctions conflict with China's Anti-Foreign Sanctions Law of 2021, and diplomatic positions taken in international bodies. Khern warns these separate decisions could be read together as a side choice, citing Australia between 2016 and 2018 backing the South China Sea arbitral ruling, declining Belt and Road Initiative endorsement, dropping an extradition treaty with China, legislating against foreign interference, and barring Huawei and ZTE from its 5G network. He notes these figures are attributed to his commentary rather than established fact. Khern frames Singapore's dependence on both powers as a sovereignty risk: the US is described as its largest foreign investor while China was its largest trading partner from 2013 to 2024, and he argues continued American presence matters because it balances China in the region. He references 1968 when Britain announced withdrawal by 1971 with Singapore having about three years to replace defence and base income that made up about a fifth of national income, presenting building capability as the response rather than asserting these historical figures independently.
items.title: Singapore's sovereignty pressures from US-China rivalry

items.summary: Anthropic closed Thursday at $97.17, down more than half from a peak that was up to 39% above its IPO price; the decline coincided with underwriters exercising their greenshoe over-allotment option. Anthropic's total capital raised reached $119.5 billion, split between $93.5 billion in the IPO and $26 billion in a concurrent private placement. The stock's debut did not lift confidence in the broader AI trade: Wall Street major indexes closed sharply lower with futures pointing to further Friday losses, while Nvidia and Meta fell more than 2% premarket, Amazon and Microsoft slipped over 1%, and AMD, SanDisk, and Intel dropped around 7%, 7%, and more than 5% respectively. The article notes near-term volatility is likely as investors reassess the IPO euphoria and question whether Anthropic can sustain a valuation of about 40 times trailing 12-month sales; this framing reflects the source's characterization rather than an established fact.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO stock fell 17% on its first day of trading

items.summary: Krishna Rao, CFO of Anthropic, and Rahul Patil, CTO, both of Indian origin, were among the seven co-founders present when Anthropic held its initial public offering on Thursday. The article frames their prominence as ironic given American political debate over immigration amid MAGA-driven xenophobia, arguing they illustrate that Indian-Americans remain central to U.S. tech primacy; this is an editorial interpretation rather than a documented fact. Rao was raised in California and attended Harvard before Yale Law School, then worked at Bain & Company, Blackstone, and Airbnb—where he helped through the pandemic and its 2020 listing—before joining Anthropic as CFO in May 2024. Patil grew up in Bengaluru, studied computer science engineering at PES University, earned a master's from Arizona State University and an MBA from the University of Washington, then worked nearly a decade at Microsoft before roles at AWS, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Stripe, where he was CTO; his last position predates Anthropic. SEC disclosures show Rao held 9,497,900 shares before the offering, sold approximately 1.66 million in the IPO, retained 7,837,991, making him the largest disclosed non-founder individual shareholder behind the seven co-founders; at Thursday's closing price that holding was worth about $762 million. The article notes other Indian-origin executives—Sid Bidasaria and Neil Shah—but states their shareholdings are not individually revealed in IPO documents, while asserting without disclosure they are all multi-millionaires.
items.title: Indian-origin executives Krishna Rao and Rahul Patil lead Anthropic at its Nasdaq IPO

items.summary: At Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference, where Jensen Huang was scheduled to speak and cochair the event but did not attend, tech leaders including Sam Altman, Clay Bavor, Jeff Bezos, Andy Jassy, Yann LeCun, Fei-Fei Li, and David Sacks were asked about his removal as Nvidia CEO. Most praised his entrepreneurship while declining to comment further on murky circumstances; Bezos said he did not know enough of the details but called Huang a remarkable founder who built a remarkable company. On X, where Huang posted Tuesday that he would return if the board decided it was in shareholders' and employees' interests, followers largely supported him with messages from Aaron Levie, Palmer Luckey, Linda Yaccarino, plus AI-generated images of Jensen as Jesus at the Last Supper or emerging from a casket. Conference speakers addressed the topic more cautiously than many X commenters, who mostly discussed Huang's alleged extramarital affair with an Nvidia business partner allegedly tied to China, questions about chips possibly being smuggled into China, and reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees rather than specifics. Despite reported board disagreement, Nvidia continues to rule out his return, which the article characterizes as fantasy even in optimistic scenarios given pending legal and geopolitical factors. The affair revelations prompted the Trump administration to tighten chip export restrictions on China; Huang agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 1; Democrats, who will regain control of both chambers in January, plan to investigate whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick facilitated diversion of Nvidia chips to China; and California's attorney general has subpoenaed Nvidia for evidence linking his affair to chips or confidential information reaching China. These are reported plans and actions attributed to their respective sources rather than established outcomes.
items.title: Silicon Valley figures praised Jensen Huang but declined to weigh in on his ouster from Nvidia

items.summary: The Associated Press reports that revelations of extramarital affairs by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, plus allegations that Alice Huang was a spy, revived online memes and videos fetishizing Asian women as spies or "trophy wives." Misa Chien, founder of The Authentic Asian, said the coverage perpetuates negative stereotypes about women who have broken ceilings. April Moh of Stand with Asian Americans reported colleagues questioning laptop security when visiting China and jokingly asking if she is a spy, while Rachel Lee noted many clients are competent yet accused of fraud or deceitfulness; Lee attributed this to a long-standing "perpetual foreigner" narrative. The annual Social Tracking of Asian Americans in the United States Index from The Asian American Foundation found at least half of U.S. adults characterized Asian Americans as respectful or reliable, while only 1 in 10 viewed them as assertive. Chien recounted being told to wear three bras to resemble Angelina Jolie's figure for a spy role ad two decades ago. Lee said Stand with Asian Americans offers education on rights and mental health support without requiring a legal case of discrimination; individuals may also set boundaries, which she called "a win-win." The article attributes broader suspicion toward Chinese people in the U.S. to heightened tensions over alien land laws, declining international student enrollment, and the first Trump administration's China Initiative, which critics say contributed to neuroscientist Jane Ying Wu's 2024 suicide after a federal investigation that never resulted in charges; Chai called this stereotype "pernicious" but inaccurate for an entire race. Attribution is throughout: figures are reported as found by The Asian American Foundation and attributed to Lee regarding Stand with Asian Americans' services, while the China Initiative link is presented as critics' claims.
items.title: Asian American women in tech and academia report renewed stereotyping after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang scandal

items.summary: OpenAI published a report titled 'Combatting adversarial distillation,' describing how it addresses the safety risks of model distillation and drawing lessons for strengthening safeguards industry-wide. The document presents attack success rate (ASR) figures from adaptive black-box red-teaming conducted against both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models, noting that a lower ASR indicates better defensive performance.
items.title: OpenAI's report on adversarial distillation defenses against GPT-6 Astra models

items.summary: Sergio Villani of Google Cloud AI argues that startups leak raw Gemini API keys as prototypes scale, and warns that a key exposed in a public repo or app bundle can be scraped within minutes and drive bills from $180 monthly into the tens of thousands. The guide's core recommendation is to eliminate bearer-token keys entirely: give each developer one login via Application Default Credentials (steps 1-2), run apps under their own service account with only roles/aiplatform.user (step 3), grant that role to a Google group for people and to the service account for apps, enforce Org Policies blocking key creation, move remaining third-party keys into Secret Manager readable by named identities, then delete every AI Studio key. Villani attributes startup billing risk specifically to the shared responsibility model under which customers pay for usage made with their own valid credentials. He notes that spend caps are currently in Preview and pause a service only after estimated cost passes a set threshold, enforcement runs on estimated rather than actual cost, overage is billed normally, and recovery can take up to an hour; he also flags Model Armor as protection against prompt injection but does not attribute specific capabilities or efficacy claims beyond screening for injection attempts. The guide presents all steps with runnable code samples in a companion repo and frames the switch as achievable without slowing prototype development.
items.title: Google's guide replaces raw Gemini API keys with identity-based access to prevent startup billing blowouts

items.summary: Apache Airflow's Managed Service offers two agentic capabilities: an in-console 'Managed Airflow Agent' that investigates failed runs and recommends fixes without changing anything, and the IDE-based Data Agent Kit plugin (using Gemini) that writes, migrates, and deploys DAGs. The post illustrates these with a fictional retailer whose hourly clickstream pipeline loads each hour's JSON files into pandas on 4 GB workers; when campaign traffic grew an hour from about 350 MB to about 1.4 GB in late October, the run failed out of memory because autoscaling adds workers but not per-task memory. The console agent correlated worker-memory metrics with task retries and recommended three fixes: loading files straight into BigQuery, batching them, or raising worker memory; it analyzed environment-wide telemetry and recommended increasing memory from 4 GB to 8 GB while flagging disabled database retention, low resilience, and no scheduled snapshots as production-readiness gaps. The agent is read-only, so the data engineer made changes herself. Because Black Friday traffic was forecast at 8 to 10 times a normal peak hour, more memory would only buy time; instead the team rebuilt for Airflow 3's native event-driven scheduling via an asset watcher and PubsubPullTrigger that process one file per task rather than a whole hour. Before migrating to Airflow 3.3.1 (composer-3-airflow-3.3.1-build.3), the agent scanned DAGs for compatibility blockers, finding a hand-run database-cleanup maintenance DAG, execution_date use in marketing_attribution, and schedule_interval usage across four other DAGs that needed renaming to schedule; it estimated effort using Data Agent Kit's migrations skill. The migration was performed on a new environment (cymbal-prod-af3) rather than in place, with the subscription capping files at 128 MB so busier hours mean more tasks instead of larger ones. A load test replaying eight times normal peak traffic showed the rebuilt pipeline running more often without changing per-task memory; all reported agent outputs and Cymbal Shops figures are illustrative because it is a fictional company. The post also notes two additional capabilities: the generally available Managed Airflow MCP server for any MCP-compatible agent (with IAM-controlled access and read-only tools flagged), and the Apache Airflow Common AI provider for model-driven tasks such as LLM-based branching, agentic retries, and schema drift detection within an Airflow 3 DAG. The authors attribute each step's value to agents working from their respective vantage points—console telemetry inspection versus IDE code review—and propose-and-decide design where the engineer reviewed every change.
items.title: Managed Airflow agents diagnose failures, size resources, and check upgrade readiness for a Black Friday clickstream pipeline

items.summary: The NIA has sent a legal assistance request to the UAE seeking copies of certain documents and permission to examine people there as part of its ongoing investigation into the mid-air attack on Indian co-pilot Smit Machchhar aboard a flydubai flight. According to agency chief Rakesh Aggarwal, who said this Friday while addressing media at an anti-terror conference in New Delhi, UAE's response is awaited and NIA will proceed once it receives the documents or permission. The attack occurred on Sept 30 when Machchhar was stabbed multiple times with a cockpit crash axe by his Omani co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami during the flight to Israel, allegedly an attempt to hijack or crash the aircraft; in response NIA registered an FIR aimed at probing what it calls a larger conspiracy behind the incident. No table of figures is presented.
items.title: NIA seeks UAE cooperation in probe of flydubai cockpit attack

items.summary: President Trump said at a White House news conference on Friday that the United States was getting close to a trade agreement with Mexico, citing cooperation over drug cartels as part of the talks. He contrasted this optimism with his characterization of negotiations with Canada as further behind, calling Prime Minister Mark Carney "very nice" but repeating claims that Canada has been "ripping us off" and asserting US self-sufficiency in cars, energy, and lumber. The statements describe Trump's own assessment rather than any concluded agreement; Mexico's President Sheinbaum said she had been told the two sides were close to an accord, while Carney indicated a deal was possible but required more work. Background context includes on-again, off-again US talks with Canada and Mexico over several months aimed at trimming American tariffs in exchange for concessions, collapsed August negotiations partly over truck tariff levels, and Trump's threat of fresh Canadian tariffs effective Jan. 1 that would open a window for renewed negotiation.
items.title: Trump says US is close to a trade deal with Mexico but less so with Canada

items.summary: The article argues that space-based data centers face an added obstacle beyond engineering and rocket availability: their debt-financed chips cannot serve as loan collateral the way terrestrial ones can. Lenders rely on repossession of chips as a backstop, which keeps borrowing cheaper; this works because even depreciated chips retain resale value, with some H100s selling for about half their 2023 cost basis and some H200 configurations at their original introduction price according to Compute Credit Index Research. Chips installed in satellites orbiting roughly 300 miles above Earth cannot be repossessed or resold if a borrower defaults, so the Financial Times reports that lenders behind SpaceX's $40 billion chip financing deal asked for none of those chips to fund orbital data center plans, though it is unclear whether SpaceX agreed. Near-term operations may not depend on this provision because SpaceX has found terrestrial compute deployment at ground stations lucrative and Musk detailed efforts to accelerate that build-out by having rocket-team engineers cast turbine blades faster than existing suppliers. Longer-term challenges remain around finding land and power for the build-out amid delays and local opposition, while open questions persist about future compute demand and buyers' ability to generate revenue. Musk began saying in early 2026 that space could become the cheapest place to operate data centers within two to three years, a claim unlikely until Starship flies fully reusable after its most recent flight test failed to recover the booster stage but landed the orbital stage at Texas; it is unclear when the second stage will fly again or how costly preparation would be. Even with such capability, SpaceX and startups including StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, and Orbital would still need to buy chips, potentially at higher cost than terrestrial equivalents, which could advantage Google's Project Suncatcher deployment of its own TPU chips in space while SpaceX and Tesla work on their chip foundry Terafab, which has not yet broken ground and will take years and billions before producing semiconductors at scale.
items.title: Space data center chip financing faces a collateral problem lenders may resist

items.summary: Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who declined to seek re-election and is being replaced by a Democrat, placed a hold on the Senate confirmation of Michael LoSapio as director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (Cisa). The block prevents the nomination from reaching an up-or-down vote in a package next month, before Republicans lose their Senate majority. Tillis told HuffPost he imposed the hold after LoSapio's Thursday hearing response to Senator Richard Blumenthal's question about whether the Capitol was attacked on January 6, 2021: LoSapio first said "I don't know," then stated "No, I don't believe it was an attack." Tillis told The Hill that acknowledging the event is not open for debate and characterized a nominee who denies it as unthoughtful. Cisa oversees protection of US election infrastructure from hacking; in 2020 it issued statements calling the election "the most secure in American history" with no evidence of tampering, while Trump then falsely claimed the count was rigged. A separate April 2025 presidential memorandum directed executive offices to address supposed risks posed by Chris Krebs, Cisa's former head, whom the memo accused of denying that the 2020 election was stolen.
items.title: Senator Tillis blocks confirmation of CISA nominee Michael LoSapio over January 6 denial

items.summary: A Missouri state court judge, Timothy Boyer of St Louis, approved on Friday a US$7.25 billion settlement between Bayer and plaintiffs alleging its weedkiller Roundup causes cancer, finding the deal 'fair, reasonable and adequate.' He overruled objections that payouts to individual victims were too low relative to earlier settlements and that delaying payments could force some claimants—including those with terminal illness—to wait an indeterminate number of years. The settlement targets roughly all current and future US claims from Bayer's approximately 65,000 Roundup lawsuits; the February announcement aimed to resolve nearly all such claims. Bayer's CEO Bill Anderson called court approval 'a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation.' The deal follows a Supreme Court ruling that overturned a US$1.25 million jury award for plaintiff John Durnell, with a 7-2 decision holding federal pesticide law barred failure-to-warn claims under state law; plaintiffs' lawyer Christopher Seeger said the ruling narrowed victims' ability to pursue court claims. The settlement excludes some pending federal cases—Bayer says about 200 remain litigated—and lawyers for objecting plaintiffs did not immediately comment. Bayer has maintained glyphosate is safe, and its share price had fallen 46% since acquiring Monsanto in 2018; the company previously settled much of the litigation for US$10.9 billion in 2020 but could not win court approval of a separate future-claims settlement worth US$1.25 billion.
items.title: Missouri judge approves Bayer's $7.25bn Roundup settlement

items.summary: Alabama Power announced Friday that its electric rates would fall across the board in January 2027, saving an estimated 1.5 million customers about $160 million annually; a household or business using 1,000 kilowatt-hours per month would save more than $50 a year versus current rates. CEO Jeff Peoples attributed the drop to projected revenue growth from large data center contracts and state economic expansion. The decrease stems from Alabama Power's formula-based Rate Stabilization and Equalization mechanism, which adjusts rates automatically each January based on company projections without formal rate case hearings; the 2027 filings project $1.76 billion in income above its PSC-set return of $1.52 billion reported through three quarters of 2026. The company also agreed to stop billing customers for part of its advertising budget from 2027, saving an average customer about four cents per month. Energy Alabama's Daniel Tait disputed the data center framing, arguing a roughly $180 million tax cut tied to nuclear credits under the Inflation Reduction Act drove most savings and that returns on equity remain above the national average; he called for lowering allowed profits rather than accepting small bill reductions. Sen. Katie Britt credited her advocacy in taking credit for lower bills following last November's Inside Climate News investigation showing Alabama Power customers paid the highest total electric bills nationally in 2024.
items.title: Alabama Power's 2027 rate decrease attributed to data centers and tax cuts amid criticism

items.summary: Balendra Shah, Nepal's 36-year-old Rastriya Swatantra Party prime minister who took office after his party swept to power in March following the Gen Z uprising that toppled K P Sharma Oli's government, is making his first high-level visit to India for a two-day trip beginning Sunday. The talks are expected to cover economic and energy cooperation, new air corridors, and reconstruction aid; Nepal's government estimates rebuilding costs nearly $5bn while pledged international aid has fallen short after the August flash floods killed more than 1,450 people. Analysts Ranjit Rae and Kanak Mani Dixit characterize the visit as an optimistic moment given the new leadership's lack of political baggage from past governments dominated by India-aligned communist parties, though they caution that Shah's young team lacks diplomatic experience with a powerful neighbour; Dixit also urged Nepal to raise its 2019 border dispute over disputed western territories. The relationship is underpinned by $9bn in bilateral trade skewed toward India and hydropower deals including up to 1,200MW of approved imports, while Shah has separately sent an 11-day delegation to China from 15 November as he balances ties with both neighbours; the real test for him will be returning with concrete financial commitments. No table is presented in the item.
items.title: Nepal's new PM Balendra Shah visits India amid hopes of a bilateral reset

items.summary: A U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit placed an administrative stay on the EPA's emergency permit, indefinitely delaying a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown that was scheduled for Friday and rescheduled by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle to Monday. The operation concerns roughly 10,000 pounds of degraded lead azide stored in 68 barrels; during a March safety review officials found the compound had dissolved into highly volatile crystals that could detonate from friction, heat or shock. Earthjustice, representing the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, filed an emergency motion less than 24 hours before the ruling, arguing the process lacked transparency and that the Army failed to adequately explore alternatives; senior attorney Thien Chau called the permit decision "abnormal and extraordinary." The court could rule on the motion within days. Lead azide is a common primary explosive in bombs. Even with blast containment barriers and water misters, experts warn the detonation would release lead-containing dust that could deposit across hundreds of miles, where tens of thousands of Iowans live; University of Iowa professor Patrick O'Shaughnessy said outdoor levels might exceed federal indoor benchmarks for homes and childcare facilities, while David Cwiertny noted farm fields cannot be wiped down. Army maps initially projected surface deposition 50 miles northwest with airborne exposure up to 100 miles away, though updated projections narrowed the range; Gov. Kim Reynolds said she had not heard of the operation until an advisory this week and asked Telle to delay it Thursday night, while Governor-elect Rob Sand and Senator-elect Josh Turek also urged postponement for more information on the decision-making process.
items.title: Federal appeals court halts Army plan to detonate unstable lead azide in Iowa

items.summary: A Friday sell-off in AI stocks pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7% to 6,910.39 (−265.44 points), its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months and marking a correction after falling over 10% from its Oct. 6 high; the Nasdaq composite fell 5.3% into negative territory for the year at 22,617.73 (−1,261.47 points), while the Dow dropped 1.9% to 48,147.33 (−949.73 points). Chip stocks bore much of the selling: Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron slid 13.9%, and Broadcom fell 12.1%. Nvidia closed 13.8% lower for its ninth decline in ten days, having dropped more than 25% since the Jensen Huang scandal; Anthropic's post-IPO stock tumbled 9.1% to $88.30 from a prior-day peak of $115.10. The rout spread globally: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5%, with European indexes also down sharply. items.title: AI-led selloff pushes S&P 500 into correction and Nasdaq negative for the year

items.summary: A Bloomberg analysis of exclusive data from property portal estie reports that rents in Katsushika, one of Tokyo's 23 wards on the city's east side, rose 23.9% over five years, the largest increase among all Tokyo wards. This gain follows decades during which prices across Japan barely moved amid deflation and renters expected housing costs to remain flat.
items.title: Katsushika leads Tokyo's rental surge amid property boom

items.summary: The article reports that police departments, militaries, and government figures produced GTA VI–styled posts to ride the game's release wave. The San Diego Police Department posted an AI-generated image of its cruiser with a sunset over San Diego Bay and the phrase 'Join San Diego PD VI,' captioned 'Want to drive a police car, we can make that happen!' A Washington state department advertised law enforcement as 'the real-life version' of GTA VI with captions about 'No cheat codes. No respawns.' Canadian departments from Edmonton to Toronto posted similar content, and the Calgary Police Service had an officer react to in-game driving clips. The Glendale Police Department advised followers to 'Keep It In The Game VI,' while Denver warned that 'Grand theft auto is still illegal.' NATO promoted its defensive alliance with military-industrial GTA-style imagery claiming 'even the best gamers would have a challenge' eluding fighter jets and submarines, and Russian army posts appeared on Telegram. A US Army battalion in Georgia granted 43 eligible soldiers four days off to play the game in exchange for reenlisting for another two years. These figures are attributed claims from an opinion piece titled 'Cops Are Pushing Extremely Corny Grand Theft Auto 6 Slop,' which frames the content as insincere engagement-seeking; no independent verification is provided, and the article's characterizations of police messaging as cringe or lacking regard for law enforcement reflect the author's view rather than established fact. The piece notes that Fox News and Elon Musk also commented on GTA VI but did not produce recruitment posts.
items.title: Police and military agencies posted GTA VI-themed recruitment content amid the game's popularity

items.summary: At a White House press conference, Trump said he would impose "tremendous penalties" on American companies that build datacenters outside the United States, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials of the plan. He argued that US-built datacenters should remain in the country because China could otherwise capture them all, while urging communities to extract concessions from developers rather than block construction. The administration separately issued new rules on Monday restricting remote access to advanced computing chips and servers to limit China's ability to train AI models; a House committee reported Wednesday that nearly 900,000 such AI chips had been sold to China in six months. Trump also dismissed reports of an Iranian plan to detonate a "dirty bomb" in Washington as a rumor he would fight if true, backed JD Vance against comments blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war, and described his relationships with Putin and Xi Jinping as fantastic despite Russia's alliance with Iran.
items.title: Trump threatens penalties on US tech firms building datacenters abroad

items.summary: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a visibly reduced welcome during her first trip to China, an event experts on Friday characterized as Beijing's "blatant" snub that may galvanize her conservative base. The visit to Shenzhen for the APEC summit was also her first face-to-face meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping since last year's remarks about Taiwan drove relations between Japan and China to historic lows. Takaichi had suggested Tokyo could intervene militarily if China attacked Taiwan, prompting a furious Beijing—which considers the island part of its territory—to impose trade restrictions and warn citizens against traveling to Japan.
items.title: Experts say China's scaled-down welcome of Takaichi could bolster her domestic standing

items.summary: A family on the outskirts of Kyiv is preparing for what they describe as the fifth winter of war against Russia, stockpiling food and fuel while attempting to maintain normalcy. The account comes from a report by NPR, which states it does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews.
items.title: Ukrainian family prepares for fifth winter of war near Kyiv

items.summary: In an episode of CGTN's The Win-Win Code, host Liu Xin visited Guangzhou-based Nexwise headquarters to tour its robotic dogs and intelligent security equipment before interviewing Chairman Sun Chao about the company's history, global ambitions, and challenges. As context for this profile, China is described as having become the world's largest exporter of AI-related goods, with Chinese tech firms expanding across Asia-Pacific markets; Nexwise is cited as an example that has brought AI data center solutions and AI-powered security technologies to more than 10 Asia-Pacific economies.
items.title: CGTN interview with Nexwise chairman on China's AI export expansion in Asia-Pacific

items.summary: At the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, President Xi Jinping offered five metaphors for Asia-Pacific cooperation: members as passengers on one ship (relevant amid rising energy and food prices squeezing household budgets while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been repeatedly shut during the US war against Iran); APEC as a multiplier holding about 40% of world population, more than 60% of global GDP and nearly half of trade; arteries of economic circulation including smart customs, transport links, cross-border payments, aligned rules and people-topeople exchanges (with few outcome documents adopted on these topics but the Chancay port in Peru inaugurated by Xi in 2024 as a maritime gateway); cooperation spreading wings like the roc with the Free Trade Area roadmap from Beijing 2014 and Putrajaya Vision 2040 setting an open, peaceful community horizon; and different paths toward one destination (tested when Xi hosted the first trilateral meeting of Chinese, Russian and American heads of state). The APEC Policy Support Unit raised its 2026 regional growth forecast to 3.4% from 3.2%, citing technology investment, while Shenzhen's trade with other APEC economies reached 3.23 trillion yuan (over $484 billion) in the first three quarters of this year, up 40%. The author notes metaphors do not cut tariffs on their own but give shared vocabulary for projects; a first audit comes next November when leaders assess whether arteries carry more and the boat rides steadier. These are the columnist's interpretations rather than established outcomes.
items.title: Xi's five metaphors frame APEC cooperation at Shenzhen summit

items.summary: A jury found Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, guilty on both federal charges in his second trial for lighting the January 1 blaze that became the Palisades Fire. The fire killed 12 people and burned neighbourhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu; prosecutors narrowed the first charge to only the initial Lachman Fire before it flared up on January 7, dropping a third timber-set charge from the retrial indictment. Prosecutors shifted strategy away from framing the crime as arson motivated by resentment toward wealthy elites, instead relying on digital forensic data placing Rinderknecht at the fire's origin, camera images of his car parked near the trailhead and phone tower movement records, testimony that he was acting erratic before the blaze, a screen-recorded video of him calling 911 more than a dozen times while asking ChatGPT whether lighting a cigarette-caused fire made one at fault, and expert testimony eliminating other ignition sources including fireworks. Defence attorney Steve Haney argued the crime scene had been compromised by six days of public access before January 7, disputed the government's identification of the origin area through his own US Forest Service expert witness, questioned missing mobile data records to prove no one else was present, urged jurors to disregard Rinderknecht's character evidence such as angry text messages, and offered fireworks as an alternative ignition source citing witnesses who heard a loud bang near the hill. Jurors were instructed not to consider the Los Angeles Fire Department's role in extinguishing the fire.
items.title: Jonathan Rinderknecht convicted of starting 2025 Palisades Fire

items.summary: For Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation 2026 in Shenzhen, CGTN and the Tengchong Scientists Forum invited young innovators from all 21 member economies to share research stories; seven featured voices were profiled across AI, health, and environment. Brandon Cho of a Republic of Korea chip design company sees room for cross-border collaboration on custom silicon despite cost and risk barriers. Adolfo De Unanue of Mexico hopes exchange programs let students form ties early using open tools and shared benchmarks. The United Nations Population Fund in Asia and the Pacific estimates one in four people in the region will be 60 or older by 2050, framing health research priorities for Zhao Peishen at Monash University, Li Hanjie in Shenzhen, and Anthony Sunjaya of Indonesia's more than 30-country projects. The World Bank estimated Peru lost $3.1 billion to its 2017 coastal El Niño event; Luis Elias Huatay Salcedo studies vegetation responses using AI, satellite imagery, and ocean temperature data, while Norulhuda Mohamed Ramli of Universiti Putra Malaysia emphasizes farmer input in shaping technology. Four leading scientists—Junying Yuan, Ingrid Daubechies, Wolfgang Baumeister, and Shing-Tung Yau—reflected on international partnerships under geopolitical strain; all four expressed hope for borderless science collaboration. The piece presents these as reported statements from the interviewees rather than verified outcomes.
items.title: CGTN profiles young APEC innovators on cross-border science collaboration

items.summary: Donald Trump announced he intends to bar US companies from constructing AI data centres abroad, warning of a "tremendous tax" for those that do so and citing fears that China would capture the technology. He described the policy as still being developed by his cabinet rather than finalized, noting in a press briefing following an Asia trip that it had not yet been formally communicated to officials. The remarks followed Washington's announcement requiring licences for firms buying advanced computer chips, intended to monitor use by Chinese companies or smuggling into China and affecting South East Asian nations investing heavily in data centres. Trump framed the stance around preventing China from overtaking the US in what he calls "super intelligence." Data centre counts are reported as approximately 3,000 operating across the US with another 1,500 under approval or construction according to Pew Research Centre figures through April; these figures represent a baseline count rather than projections. The policy's enforcement remains unclear, and it would impact companies such as Meta, which broke ground on an external data centre in Alberta, Canada, and Google, which announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in Finland including three data centres, two of whose construction projects were halted over forest clearance concerns. The BBC contacted both Meta and Google for comment.
items.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas

items.summary: On Nov. 19, the US government auctioned off 12.7 million hectares (31.5 million acres) of American Samoan seabed for $6 million, even though a federal court in Hawaiʻi had ruled on Nov. 16 that the sale violated the Endangered Species Act by failing to account for impacts on endangered species. The auction was won by Wetstone U.S. Ventures at the starting price of $3 million per lease (approximately 19 US cents per acre), with only one bidder participating after two companies registered interest; it granted exploration rights and marks the first completed seabed mineral-lease auction globally. Chris Eaton, senior attorney at Earthjustice which represented the plaintiffs, called the decision to proceed "lawless" while noting a second pending motion could invalidate the process and any leases issued. The sale proceeds despite American Samoa's 2024 moratorium on deep-sea mining within 3 nautical miles of its coast, with US jurisdiction extending over the remaining exclusive economic zone out to 200 nautical miles; critics warn it threatens the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument and local cultural, food security and economic interests. The MMA defends the activity as necessary for national-security minerals such as those used in fighter jets and renewable energy technologies, following a Trump administration executive order from April 2025 to accelerate deep-sea mining. A CNMI lease sale covering 27 million hectares (67 million acres) is scheduled for Dec. 16.
items.title: US auctions American Samoan seabed despite court ruling it illegal
