items.summary: In Meta's November 19, 2026 sustainability report, executives Rachel Peterson and Blair Swedeen announced a re-evaluation of the company's timelines, sequencing, interim milestones, and specifically its 2030 net-zero target. They attributed this reconsideration to AI infrastructure demand growing faster than projected, noting that 'our long-term ambitions haven't changed, but our operating environment has.' Meta's total emissions rose from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025, a surge the company linked largely to capital goods such as data center servers; this footprint is roughly comparable to that of Idaho and exceeds states including Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. This public acknowledgment stands out because Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have so far maintained their original sustainability goals, though all four companies acknowledge challenges from hyperscale data-center buildouts and continue operating AI facilities powered by natural gas.
items.title: Meta reconsiders its 2030 net-zero goal after record AI-driven emissions growth

items.summary: Young protesters gathered beneath Berlin's television tower to oppose rising defence budgets and a potential return of compulsory military service, chanting 'Never again conscription' while carrying signs reading 'Hands off my future.' One participant stated the group was resisting because it concerns their future. The demonstration occurred alongside youth-led rallies in Rome, Frankfurt, and London on a broader day of European protests, though local grievances differed across locations; participants shared anger at political leaders they accused of sidelining their generation amid increasing military spending.
items.title: Berlin students protest German rearmament and possible conscription

items.summary: The bipartisan energy permitting reform bill passed the Senate 62-33, but tribal sovereignty over development beyond reservation boundaries under the National Historic Preservation Act became a central concern. The NHPA requires federal agencies to consult tribes without their consent, and some tribal organizations argue the bill's changes would weaken that consultation process; large projects like the SunZia transmission line have drawn prior pushback despite such reviews. In response, the Senate amended the bill's initial NHPA language over sections weakening tribal consultation and permitting Interior Department oversight of Tribal Historic Preservation Offices, though a bipartisan amendment to further strengthen consultation negotiated by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) failed after Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) attempted to scuttle the bill; as of Friday, groups including the National Congress of American Indians and NATHPO remained opposed. Tribal issues are expected to weigh on House negotiations amid pressure from supporters for swift passage before this congressional session ends, making substantive amendments unlikely. Views diverge: some organizations see opportunities in tribal energy sovereignty, with the National Tribal Energy Association supporting provisions it said would streamline infrastructure deployment and unlock Tribal energy potential, while the Apsáalooke (Crow) Nation submitted a letter of support citing bureaucratic delays; NoiseCat argued tribes are not uniformly anti-development and that framing them as environmental allies obscures their complexity.
items.title: Tribal sovereignty concerns reshaped Senate permitting reform bill and may shape House debate

items.summary: A Moscow court sentenced Sofia Rosenfeld, daughter of ornithologist Boris Rosenfeld, to three and a half years in a penal colony for financing extremism. The charge traces to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which Russian authorities designated as extremist after designating it so in summer 2021; Sofia had been on an Arctic expedition without phone or internet access at the time and only stopped donating upon returning to Moscow. Prosecutors requested five years, but friends expected a fine because independent outlet Mediazona calculated that about 85% of convictions across roughly 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have resulted in non-custodial sentences; Sofia nonetheless received custodial time. The family and colleagues say her donations were not political activism but support for anti-corruption work, and they are campaigning for the sentence to be overturned through an appeal signed by more than 1,000 people addressed to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights. Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to Sofia in detention; she holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship and her family hopes Israel will help bring her back.
items.title: Sofia Rosenfeld jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation

items.summary: UN human rights experts called on Iran to end what they describe as an escalation in persecution of independent lawyers, warning that restricting access to legal representation raises the risk of arbitrary detention, coerced confessions and unfair trials. The experts' statement came in mid-November; between September 2025 and September 2026 at least 135 lawyers were issued summonses or arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling, and 23 including five women were reportedly arrested after nationwide protests in January and February 2026. Human rights lawyer Sina Yousefi said the security services, judiciary and prosecution apparatus increasingly used targeted measures against independent lawyers defending politically persecuted people; he was himself arrested in October 2022 during the 'Woman Life Freedom' protests and sentenced to six months for propaganda against the system before leaving Iran. Shabnam Moinipour of the Center for Supporters of Human Rights said restricting a defendant's right to choose their own lawyer undermines defense, noting that lawyers are often only granted access to files after preliminary investigations conclude; she called this practice incompatible with Iran's UN Human Rights Committee obligations and described it as producing a chilling effect. The article attributes these assessments to Yousefi, Moinipour, the CSHR organization, and reports by the Defenders of Human Rights Center and IBAHRI.
items.title: UN experts warn of escalating repression against Iranian lawyers

items.summary: In a satirical piece, journalist Barney Ronay contends that tech billionaires applying artificial intelligence to sports represent a greater threat than rogue robots. He frames Jensen Huang as irreplaceable at Nvidia while noting the irony of technology designed to eliminate jobs; he asserts his own theory that AI may save rather than destroy humanity because it lacks desires and drives for power. The central concern centers on Major League Cricket's San Francisco Unicorns, founded by Anand Rajaraman and Venky Harinarayan as a "startup"-style team using real-time tactical tools called Cric Lens with what they describe as Human-in-the-Loop Execution; Ronay quotes Finn Allen describing the system as providing "the perfect amount of contribution." He characterizes AI-assisted captaincy decisions as potentially brain-doping and argues that big tech's interest in sport, such as Bezos at Liverpool, is a hedge against job loss. Quoting an unnamed Unicorns founder claiming cricket could expand to football and soccer, Ronay rejects this expansion, arguing AI would destroy the human elements of sport like hunch-based scouting rather than improve it; he asserts that watching AI-managed Manchester United would lack cultural value or capacity to surprise viewers. He frames opposition as Luddite but claims the historical movement had valid points about industrialization's effects on quality and happiness.
items.title: Barney Ronay argues AI-driven cricket threatens sport's human value

items.summary: The ABQ BioPark BUGarium in Albuquerque, New Mexico, closed for about a year and reopened in October 2026 following an approximately $1.45 million renovation (a claim attributed to the source). The facility is part of a larger complex that also includes an aquarium, traditional zoo, and botanic garden. Curator of entomology Alexandra Miller told Mongabay by email that visitors arrive with attitudes ranging from disgust to fascination, and she said guests should learn how arthropods support ecosystems, help native populations, and require specialized care comparable to gorillas and elephants (an unverified comparison). The BUGarium's stated purpose is public education about insects' ecological roles. A featured exhibit shows a leaf-cutter ant colony from Trinidad housed in blown-glass chambers that display the fungus-farming society; it also exhibits species from New Mexico's Chihuahuan Desert. Miller described connecting guests to nature as central to the BioPark, and said the BUGarium is among a small number of U.S. facilities with live insect and arthropod exhibits (San Diego Zoo and Cincinnati Zoo are named as examples). The E.O. Wilson quote about wiping out insects was included by the source but not attributed to him in-text beyond being called 'famed entomologist.'
items.title: ABQ BioPark's BUGarium reopened after a renovation to focus on insects and arthropods

items.summary: Crude traded in a tight range on Friday, with Brent up 0.22% to $92.18 per barrel and WTI gaining 0.35% to $82.73, both well below October levels above $110 but little changed from the week's start. The International Energy Agency projects a global oil surplus of 1.7 million bpd in Q4 2026 against demand of 104.3 million bpd, reversing its prior deficit forecast after raising supply estimates by 3.3 million bpd and cutting OPEC crude call to 20.8 million bpd; the EIA forecasts rising U.S. stocks averaging 3.5 million bpd in early 2027 as Gulf shut-in production fell from a May peak of 10.9 million bpd, while OPEC+ output rose roughly 2 million bpd in October led by Saudi Arabia and Iraq. Standard Chartered cautions that tanker shortages, damaged infrastructure, record freight rates, and thin inventories still constrain shipments reaching buyers, warns the IEA's surplus call exceeds any other agency's with past surpluses often failing to materialize on schedule, notes OPEC forecasts 2027 demand at 108.3 million bpd versus the IEA's lower figure, and expects continued Middle East attacks and stalled talks to sustain a geopolitical premium while crude falls through 2027 as supply normalizes; in natural gas, Standard Chartered sees elevated European prices into winter despite milder weather and better LNG supply, with EU inventories at 70.4% on Nov. 15 versus the five-year average about 18 points lower, Qatar's October LNG exports roughly doubling yet remaining two-thirds below pre-war levels under a force majeure through December, and Dutch TTF front-month futures rising €2.25 to €83.10 per megawatt-hour on a Norway Troll field outage and cooler forecasts.
items.title: Oil prices narrow as agency surplus forecasts offset Middle East geopolitical premium

items.summary: A study published this month in the Journal of Environmental Studies and Sciences surveyed 516 people aged 18-28 in Colombia's Antioquia subregion (Aburrá Valley) on how they feel about climate change. More than 85% said they felt affected by it, while nearly three-quarters described the future as frightening; still, slightly more than half leaned toward optimism and around 90% wanted to take action. The most intense emotions reported were sadness (86.2%), fear (81.8%), powerlessness (77.7%) and guilt (76.4%). Co-author Alejandro Álvarez-Vanegas of EAFIT University in Medellín described a sense of moral injury toward decision-makers, with respondents feeling both betrayed by institutions and personally responsible when responsibility is framed as individual rather than economic or political behavior; 59% felt unprotected by local governments and around 62% by businesses. The researchers also noted that most climate mental-health research concentrates in the Global North, citing a bibliometric analysis of 1,570 publications dominated by high-income English-speaking institutions, and said their work aims to guide policies rather than leave young people feeling powerless; they are planning a follow-up study on emotions before and after educational initiatives. The findings reflect survey responses attributed to participants and the researchers' interpretation, not established fact about climate change itself.
items.title: Colombian youth link climate change to mental distress, yet remain willing to act

items.summary: On November 20, a US federal judge sentenced Nikhil Gupta to 19 years and seven months in prison before ordering his deportation to India. The sentence followed Gupta's February guilty plea to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering; sentencing had been postponed three times since the plea. Prosecutors characterized Gupta as an active participant who acted on directions from Vikash Yadav, a former Indian intelligence officer and employee of India's cabinet secretariat, whom they allege directed him to kill Pannun based on political ideology. Defense argued Gupta was merely an intermediary acting under pressure rather than central to the plot. The conspiracy allegedly began in May 2023 when Yadav recruited Gupta; Gupta then approached a man he believed to be a drug trafficker who was actually DEA confidential informant 'Pacho Sanchez,' which introduced him to undercover agent 'Carlos' posing as a hitman. Prosecutors allege Yadav and Gupta agreed to pay $100,000 for the killing and delivered $15,000 as an advance payment on or about June 9, 2023. Communications seized by Czech law enforcement after Gupta's arrest in Prague show he also discussed targeting Hardeep Singh Nijjar following that man's June 18, 2023 death outside a gurudwara in Surrey, British Columbia; transcripts include Gupta telling the agent they had 'so many target' and instructing him to kill Pannun before the 29th. Prosecutors also allege planning of another murder in Nepal or Pakistan around May-June 2023, an offer by Yadav on June 22, 2023 to arrange sales of AK-56 rifles and M20 pistols for profit, and offers to arrange airport clearance at Imphal, Manipur. Gupta was arrested in the Czech Republic on June 30, 2023, extradited to the US in June 2024, and pleaded guilty on February 13 of this year. Yadav remains at large after being charged in the US; his whereabouts are unknown following bail in April 2024 for a separate Delhi kidnapping and extortion case. Indian authorities have called claims about India's involvement 'fabricated and malicious' and have not commented on the sentencing, while the US State Department has yet to accede to India's request to designate Pannun as a terrorist despite his role with Sikhs For Justice, which was designated a terrorist organization in India in 2019. In court Gupta apologized, saying he 'own[s] it completely,' and outside the courtroom Khalistan supporters gathered around 200 people chanting slogans, erected cutouts of Indian officials Modi, Shah, and Jaisankar in prison clothes with handcuffs, and filmed tearing the Indian national flag while chanting 'Balkanise India.' Pannun attended a hero's welcome before sitting on the third row with a bodyguard. The article reports these events as alleged facts drawn from court filings, transcripts, and statements; it does not establish that any killing occurred or confirm Yadav's identity beyond US authorities' characterization of him as a former Indian intelligence officer.
items.title: Nikhil Gupta sentenced to 19 years and seven months for plot to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.

items.summary: Andy Burnham announced that the UK will discuss options for even closer ties with the EU following an agreement covering British food exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme. The deal scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK adopting some EU regulations from 2028 was described by Burnham as delivering what polling suggests the public want; critics countered that it would make the UK a rule taker rather than a rule maker. A youth mobility scheme allows up to 100,000 young people aged 18 to 31 on each side to travel, work and study for up to three years, with opportunities targeted by no later than January 2030; talks on tuition fees remain open through a further six months. Talks concluding the emissions-trading linkage aim to apply from 2028, and both sides committed to cooperating against migrant smuggling while sharing law-enforcement data. The Treasury's analysis was cited as suggesting the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year; Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch disputed this figure, claiming modelling she had seen put it at 0.0%, while Nigel Farage and Ed Davey called the arrangement an unfair betrayal or insufficient. Legislation is expected in Parliament next week, with Burnham noting these agreements may be the limit achievable in this Parliament before a long-term relationship is decided after the election due by August 2029.
items.title: UK to explore closer EU ties after agreeing trade, mobility and emissions-deal stages

items.summary: On 20th November 2026, mathematician Ravi Vakil posted an announcement on his blog describing a proposed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis attributed to Alessandro Masullo. According to Vakil, Brian Conrad has been reviewing the work for months and provided extensive feedback that is being incorporated, with results so far looking promising. The effort is described as entirely human, involving no AI assistance. Originally, plans had included bringing Masullo to Stanford for a year to polish the writing before announcing it after further review by additional people; Vakil now states it seems best to release the current draft instead. All claims about the proof's validity and status are attributed solely to Vakil as an unverified source.
items.title: Ravi Vakil announces a draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis by Alessandro Masullo

items.summary: Gen. Rob Magowan, head of the UK's Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, publicly confirmed for the first time that the National Cyber Force carries out offensive cyber missions against state adversaries he named as Russia, China, Iran and North Korea. Speaking to Sky News in his first interview since assuming the four-star role earlier this year, Magowan said these states are 'a threat to our way of life' and conduct operations in the cyber domain, adding that there will be a cost for them doing so. He also stated the force targets organized crime groups and individuals engaged in harmful online activity affecting children. The remarks followed King Charles's official opening earlier this week of the National Cyber Force's new headquarters in Samlesbury, Lancashire; much of its work is conducted from UK facilities including Ribble House. Magowan said the force uses computer network exploitation to understand an adversary's architecture and achieve effect inside hostile networks, describing Britain's cyber threat as 'significant' while noting operational details remain largely classified.
items.title: UK confirms National Cyber Force conducts offensive cyber operations against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea

items.summary: At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, a draft agreement presented to nearly 200 countries omitted any reference to fossil fuels while pledging support for carbon-capture technology. European nations criticized the text as casting the summit as a 'fossil-fuel COP' and warned of talks ending without an agreed deal absent substantial changes; German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider attributed resistance to parties profiting from avoiding the term, per Bloomberg's reporting. The draft proposed capturing at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide by 2035 toward a goal of 2.5 gigatons, though fewer than 0.2% of fossil-fuel emissions are currently captured according to the Global Carbon Budget; negotiators were told removing this language is not an option but neither is adding transition language away from fossil fuels. Panama's environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro accused COP31 of being held hostage by a 'petroleum mafia' and threatened to withhold support for any final deal, while Palau's Ilana Seid described positions as hardening with little room for movement; these are attributed claims reported through Bloomberg rather than independently verified outcomes.
items.title: COP31 delegates clash over fossil-fuel language in climate draft
